writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for Cabinet Office, what steps are being taken to secure open-source software supply chains used across government and critical infrastructure.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Individual departments and contracting authorities remain responsible for their specific software architecture, operational lifecycle and security requirements when managing open-source software supply chains.

To support them, the Government Commercial Agency enforces baseline supplier integrity and cyber security standards at the commercial level, providing assured routes to procure and deploy technology securely across the public sector in alignment with National Cyber Security Centre guidance.
writtenQuestions.heading: Software: Supply Chains

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, whether the Cabinet Office maintains a central register of all social media content creators, digital agencies, and influencers remunerated by government departments; and whether she plans to publish itemised departmental spend on influencer marketing.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
An overview of influencer marketing is held by our creative agency.

There are currently no plans to publish an itemised list of departmental spend on influencer marketing.
writtenQuestions.heading: Government Departments: Social Media

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, pursuant to the answer to Question 38199, whether the discussions with US counterparts referred to have included the security of AI models developed in China.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
I refer the Hon. Member to the answer given on 16 November 2026 to Question 38199.

The United Kingdom and the United States share a strong partnership rooted in our shared values and people-to-people links, and demonstrated by our close collaboration on security, defence, trade and technology.

Ministers and officials have regular discussions with US counterparts on a range of technology and security issues. However, details of confidential government-to-government discussions are not routinely disclosed.
writtenQuestions.heading: Artificial Intelligence: Cybersecurity

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, whether the Prime Minister's AI Taskforce will publish an annual report.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Prime Minister’s AI Taskforce sets the overall direction of the Government’s AI strategy and its remit is to unlock opportunities for economic growth, prosperity, and public sector transformation, operating as an empowered unit to deliver tangible public outcomes.

To maintain an agile focus on delivery, the Taskforce does not intend to publish formal annual reports. Updates on its progress and key milestones will be communicated to Parliament and the public as and when appropriate.
writtenQuestions.heading: AI Taskforce

writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText: The AI Biosecurity Lab will be independent of Government. The Government will work with the Lab to ensure it has robust security arrangements in place. This includes a thorough assessment of the security implications of any technology before it is approved for use. Where the Lab works with Government Departments, it will also follow applicable Departmental security and information-handling requirements.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, what steps he is taking to protect consumers in Scotland from subscription traps.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government is committed to protecting consumers across the UK, including in Scotland, from subscription traps. The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 introduces new protections to give consumers greater transparency and control over subscription contracts. These include clearer information before entering a contract, reminders before certain renewal payments, cooling-off rights, and straightforward arrangements for cancelling subscriptions. We anticipate these measures will provide £436 million of consumer benefit per year.

Subject to Parliamentary approval, the new regime will come into force on 1 January 2027. Guidance has also been produced to help businesses prepare for and comply with the new requirements.
writtenQuestions.heading: Internet: Subscriptions

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, what assessment he has made of the potential impact of Royal Mail's new delivery model entitled DM26 on older and digitally excluded residents in rural communities, including those who rely on timely postal communications.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government remains committed to ensuring a reliable and accessible universal postal service for users across the UK, including in rural areas.

Ofcom’s changes to Royal Mail’s USO requirements are intended to meet customer needs, improve reliability of postal services and safeguard the long-term future of the universal postal service. Realising those benefits depends on Royal Mail implementing the reforms operationally through its new delivery model, agreed with the Communication Workers Union (CWU).

The Secretary of State and I met Royal Mail and the CWU on 3 November 2026, stressing the importance of management and the workforce working together constructively to improve the service going forward.
writtenQuestions.heading: Postal Services: Rural Areas

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, whether he has considered asking the Competition and Markets Authority to conduct a Strategic Market Status investigation of the social media services provided by Meta, following the publication of its revised commercial terms on 30 October 2026.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
As an independent authority, the Competition and Markets Authority is responsible for operating the digital markets regime, including taking decisions on whether to open Strategic Market Status investigations.

On 30 October, the CMA opened an investigation into Meta’s commercial terms using its Competition Act 1998 powers.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, how many of the AI training courses completed through the AI Skills Boost programme by the end of July 2026 were completed by employees of the programme's delivery partners.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The AI Skills Boost programme is delivered through a voluntary partnership of 32 industry and public sector organisations, which provide free AI training to workers across the UK.

Our partners reported more than 2.2 million AI training course completions by the end of July 2026, rising to over 2.7 million by the end of September 2026.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, whether he has considered protections for workers in AI frontier companies who public raise concerns for AI safety in these powerful organisations.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
To qualify for whistleblowing protection under the Employment Rights Act 1996, a worker must reasonably believe that their disclosure tends to show one or more of the types of wrongdoing listed in the Act. These include criminal offences, breaches of legal obligations, and risks to health and safety.

The government has not made a specific assessment of the protections for workers in frontier AI companies who raise concerns about AI safety. However, it is currently consulting on whether the existing categories of wrongdoing remain appropriate, including in relation to emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence. The consultation closes on 8 January.
writtenQuestions.heading: Artificial Intelligence: Safety

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what steps they are taking to secure mutual recognition of qualifications with the European Union in support of the United Kingdom’s position as a global leader in the artificial intelligence sector.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government remains committed to strengthening recognition of professional qualifications with the EU. These arrangements enable skilled professionals to provide their services more easily across the UK and EU, supporting the UK’s global standing in regulated service sectors.

At the UK-EU Summit on 20 November 2026, the UK and EU committed to expedite negotiations on a UK-EU architects recognition arrangement and work together to explore recognition arrangements for other professions. The UK government encourages and supports all UK regulators to use the Trade and Cooperation Agreement framework to pursue mutual routes for recognition.
writtenQuestions.heading: Artificial Intelligence: Qualifications

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what discussions she has had with Ofcom regarding evidence submitted to the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee on 10 November 2026 on whether platforms are giving sufficient weight to freedom of expression when implementing duties under the Online Safety Act 2023.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Safeguards for freedom of expression have been built into the framework of the Online Safety Act, which places duties on platforms to protect users’ rights to freedom of expression when introducing safety measures. The Act places additional duties on Category 1 services requiring providers to carry out, update and publish assessments on the impact of safety measures and policies on freedom of expression and privacy.

Ministers and officials meet regularly with Ofcom to discuss the implementation of the Online Safety Act. The Government remains committed to ensuring that the Act's safeguards for freedom of expression are upheld.
writtenQuestions.heading: Internet: Freedom of Expression

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what assessment she has made of the cost to the UK economy of the Microsoft 365 Services outage from November 12-13 2026.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The full impacts of the Microsoft outage are still emerging, so no such assessment has been made. We expect Microsoft to share their lessons learned from this incident. We will be engaging further on how they will prevent such incidents happening in the future and plan for swifter remediation of incidents to limit service disruption.

Cloud computing services are regulated under the Security of Network & Information Systems Regulations (2018) (the “NIS Regulations”). We expect a report would have been lodged with the regulator (the Information Commission) and for the regulator to be reviewing that report, however they would not be able to publicly comment on specific regulatory investigations.
writtenQuestions.heading: Microsoft: Outages

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what recent discussions she has had with social media companies on their responsibilities regarding removal of illegal content.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText: The Secretary of State, Ministers and officials regularly engage with social media companies on online safety, including their responsibilities to tackle illegal content. Under the Online Safety Act, platforms must have proportionate systems and processes to prevent users encountering illegal content and remove it swiftly once aware.
writtenQuestions.heading: Social Media: Crime

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what recent steps have been taken alongside (a) social media companies and (b) artificial intelligence companies to (i) prevent and (ii) remove AI-generated child sexual abuse images from social media platforms.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
AI-generated child sexual abuse material is abhorrent and illegal. Under the Online Safety Act it is priority illegal content, so in-scope services must proactively prevent users encountering it. Services must also swiftly remove illegal content once identified.

To tackle it at source, the Crime and Policing Act 2026 criminalised AI models optimised to create this material and gave government a power to bring currently unregulated AI chatbots into scope of the Act’s illegal content duties.
writtenQuestions.heading: Child Sexual Abuse Material: Artificial Intelligence

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, whether the Government Digital Service holds a record of the AI models used by government departments.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
There is currently no central tracking of use of models within government, but there is a relevant initiative focused on algorithmic transparency and some further planned activity in the Cabinet Office.

For tools that have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or directly interact with the public, government publishes information via the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS). The ATRS captures comprehensive information about algorithmic tools, including about the models they are built on, their design, purpose, governance, and role in decision-making. Publication of records is mandatory for central government and arm's length bodies that deliver front line services, and it is recommended best practice for the wider public sector.

ATRS records are published on GOV.UK. At time of writing, 157 records have been published since the Standard was first launched in 2021. These come from a wide variety of government departments and agencies, with more being added every month. HMG departments are required to identify and produce records for all tools that fall in scope of the ATRS. The Government Digital Service regularly check with departments to ensure that this is on track.

This approach aims to deliver meaningful transparency, where the general public can access high-level explanations quickly and easily, and specialised or interested parties can explore more detailed information as they wish.

The Cabinet Office Future Civil Service team are looking to create a centralised view on AI deployment across departments. The recently established the GovAI Unit within the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, will coordinate, develop and scale AI solutions across Government in collaboration with the Prime Minister’s AI Taskforce. The Government is committed to the ethical and transparent deployment of AI with appropriate guardrails, as our overriding principle.
writtenQuestions.heading: Artificial Intelligence: Government Departments

askingMember.name: Dame Chi Onwurah
askingMember.memberFrom: Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what recent discussions has she had with Ofcom on the regulator’s pace in enforcing anti-fraud duties under the Online Safety Act; and when does the Department expect Ofcom to begin penalising platforms that expose consumers to online scams.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Decisions on whether to investigate, enforce, or sanction regulated services are for the independent regulator. The government has been clear that effective enforcement of Online Safety Act duties is a priority. Ministers and officials meet regularly with Ofcom to discuss the implementation and enforcement of the Act.

The Act lists certain fraud offences as ‘priority offences’, meaning regulated services must prevent users encountering user-generated fraudulent content, swiftly remove it if it appears, and manage risks of their services facilitating fraud. Additional duties for Category 1 and 2A services to tackle paid-for fraudulent advertising are expected to be in effect in 2027.
writtenQuestions.heading: Internet: Fraud

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the merits of requiring licensing agreements to train AI models on copyrighted music in the UK.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText: The Government recognises the importance of fair licensing so that musicians and creators are paid when their work trains AI models. As set out in the March report on AI and Copyright, the Government supports licensing and continues to engage across the creative industries to consider how best to help rightsholders control and license their work. This work includes reviewing technical solutions that creators can use to control their works online, standards and best practice on input transparency. This will help inform whether Government intervention is needed, and what a proportionate approach might look like.
writtenQuestions.heading: Music: Artificial Intelligence

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the legal liability of AI agents, particularly in instances of AI hallucination.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the potential for harm where AI systems, including AI agents, produce inaccurate or misleading outputs. Existing legal and regulatory frameworks apply to the development and use of AI systems, including AI agents. Whether liability arises in a particular case, including where harm results from an inaccurate or misleading output, will depend on the facts, the applicable law and the responsibilities of the parties involved.

The Government continues to consider how existing frameworks apply as AI systems become more capable and autonomous. Where the evidence shows that changes are necessary to ensure the safety of the British public, we will act.
writtenQuestions.heading: Artificial Intelligence

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what assessment her Department has made of trends in the level of teacher recruitment and retention challenges in specialist subjects, including modern foreign languages, music and digital skills, ahead of the implementation of the reformed Key Stage 3 curriculum.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department recognises the value of strong teachers working in every classroom across key stage 3 and key stage 4. That is why we have recruited more than 3,000 new secondary teachers, continue to invest in initial teacher training and have set out plans through the Schools White Paper for a Teacher Training Entitlement, so that every teacher can access high-quality professional development.

Our schoolteacher pipeline is also growing, with nearly 32,600 new entrants to Initial Teacher Training (ITT) in Autumn 2025, up 13% from the previous year. There were 17,200 entrants to secondary postgraduate ITT (PGITT) courses in the 2025/26 academic year, 1,900 more than in the 2024/25 academic year.

Modern foreign languages had 1,378 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, compared with 1,179 in 2024/25, which is a 17% increase.

Music had 369 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, compared with 345 in 2024/25, which is a 7% increase.

Computing had 723 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, a 46% increase on 2024/25. This is the highest number of computing PGITT entrants since comparable statistics began in 2012/13.
writtenQuestions.heading: Teachers: Labour Turnover and Recruitment

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government when they plan to hold a consultation on their proposal for an education technology certification scheme; and when they anticipate that scheme becoming operational.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department launched its consultation on the proposed education technology and artificial intelligence product safety certification scheme on 10 November 2026. The consultation closes on 4 February 2027, and the government intends to publish its response in spring 2027.

Subject to the outcome of the consultation, it is likely that a minimum of 18 months would be needed to establish the product certification scheme, before products could be certified, followed by a transition period to allow adoption by suppliers and education settings.
writtenQuestions.heading: Education: Technology

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government whether participation in the proposed education technology (EdTech) certification scheme will be mandatory or voluntary for suppliers of EdTech products.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department launched its consultation on the proposed education technology and artificial intelligence product safety certification scheme on 10 November 2026. Under the proposals set out for consultation, the certification scheme would not initially be mandatory. The department does not currently have specific powers to require suppliers to obtain certification or education settings to use certified products.

The department proposes instead to set a clear expectation through statutory guidance that education settings should obtain proportionate assurance that products within the scheme’s scope meet the relevant safety standards. Certification would ordinarily provide that assurance, while allowing settings to rely on equivalent evidence where this is justified. The consultation also seeks views on whether legislative underpinning may be needed in future.
writtenQuestions.heading: Education: Technology

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government whether the standards assessed by the proposed education technology certification scheme will include (1) children’s physical and mental health implications, (2) data privacy implications, and (3) superiority of learning outcomes.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department launched its consultation on the proposed education technology and artificial intelligence product safety certification scheme on 10 November 2026. Under the proposals set out for consultation, products would be assessed against a range of criteria including data privacy, and children’s mental health and cognitive, social and emotional development. The consultation also seeks views on whether there are additional risks that the scheme proposal currently does not cover.

Physical health is not proposed as a separate certification criterion and certification would not assess a product’s overall educational effectiveness, except where a lack of effectiveness could put children at risk of harm.

The department will continue to support settings to make evidence-informed decisions about product effectiveness through guidance and evidence on what works, including the EdTech Testbed programme in partnership with the Education Endowment Foundation.
writtenQuestions.heading: Education: Technology

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the potential impact of any social media ban for people aged under 16 on the delivery of the Pearson BTEC Level 1/Level 2 Tech Award in Creative Media Production and the proposed GCSE in Creative Media Production.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The specifications for the Pearson BTEC Level 1/Level 2 Technical Award in Creative Media Production are developed by the awarding organisation, Pearson, in line with the department’s technical guidance and approval requirements.

The department has engaged with Ofqual and awarding organisations on the potential impact of the proposed social media ban. While some qualifications may use social media as part of teaching, learning or assessment activities, the department has not identified any changes to qualification content that would be required as a result of the proposed restrictions.

Awarding organisations are responsible for qualification specifications and assessment requirements. The department will continue to work with Ofqual and awarding organisations to ensure that qualifications remain valid, deliverable and fit for purpose.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, what assessment she has made of the potential impact of Ofgem’s proposed Data Centre Commitment Fee on the UK’s competitiveness as a destination for data centre investment relative to other countries.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, whether his Department collects data on the employment outcomes of workers made redundant from technology and digital occupations, including (a) the average length of time before securing new employment and (b) changes in earnings following re-employment; and what support his Department provides to such workers who remain unemployed six months after redundancy.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Department for Work and Pensions monitors data published by the independent Office for National Statistics on the estimated number of redundancies by industry. Such industries include ‘Information & communication’ and ‘Professional, Scientific & Technical Activities’. This data may be accessed using this link: RED02: Redundancies by age, industry and region - Office for National Statistics

The Department provides support to employers and individuals affected by redundancy through its Rapid Response Service. The service aims to help people move quickly into alternative employment and can provide tailored support including help with job search and CVs, identifying transferable skills, accessing appropriate training and overcoming barriers to securing new employment. Support can begin when an individual is under threat of redundancy or during their notice period and can normally continue for up to 13 weeks following redundancy, whether or not the individual makes a claim to benefit.

The Department also reviews published data on the duration of Universal Credit (UC) claims, and the rate at which UC customers in the ‘searching for work’ conditionality regime enter employment. This analysis can be accessed using this link: Get Britain Working: Labour Market Insights October 2026 - GOV.UK

The Department for Work and Pensions offers a range of employment support, including the ‘Find a Job’ website, financial support through the Flexible Support Fund to help with interviews or starting work, and tailored, flexible support through Jobcentre Plus. Where appropriate, Work Coaches identify skill gaps and signpost jobseekers to relevant training and provision, such as Skills Bootcamps, apprenticeships, sector-based work academy programmes, and free courses for jobs, as well as essential English, maths and digital skills. For those who have been on Universal Credit for 6 months or more, the Restart Scheme provides 12 months of more intensive support, including bespoke action plans.

The DWP Careers Service in England provides free, impartial careers support through to anyone who is looking for work, who wants to get on in work, or who wants to change their career or retrain, regardless of whether they are claiming benefits. Careers information and advice is available via the digital offer, Get Careers Information and Advice.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what steps his Department is taking to help increase levels of uptake of Pension Credit.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText: We launched the latest phase of the Pension Credit take-up campaign in October. It includes new advertising across television, radio, print and social media, supported by media partnerships and social media influencers. For Pension Credit week of action, we distributed 660,000 leaflets to selected households and continue to work with partners and local authorities to support the campaign.
writtenQuestions.heading: Pension Credit

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what steps they are taking to fill shortages in the supply of labour required for the construction and maintenance of AI data centres, including through training.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText: DWP’s Strategic Relationship Team works with employers and sector bodies to understand skills shortages and develop recruitment and training pathways that better connect Jobcentre customers to employer demand. In the construction sector, SRT works with the Construction Industry Training Board (CITB) to promote routes into construction careers, including apprenticeships, pre-employment training and Sector-based Work Academy Programmes (SWAPs). This includes helping to make these routes accessible to customers looking to retrain for skilled occupations, such as electricians, by connecting them to the most appropriate programmes and opportunities available.
writtenQuestions.heading: Data Centres: Skilled Workers

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what steps they take to ensure that the health and circumstances information held on Universal Credit claimant records is accurate and kept up to date, in line with Article 5(1)(d) of the UK GDPR.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, (a) what standards will govern the inclusion or exclusion of detailed psychotherapy and psychological therapy session notes relating to children in the Single Patient Record and (b) what assessment has been made of whether existing shared care records apply equivalent safeguards.

writtenQuestions.answerText:
In respect of the Single Patient Record, discussions are ongoing on a range of practical issues about its scope and operation, and that includes determining what arrangements should apply to the sharing of psychotherapy and psychological therapy records, including the highly personal and private information contained in the notes of therapy sessions.

No final decisions have been made in this area, and we are extremely mindful of the views of patient groups, therapy professionals and other stakeholders, and of the debates that have previously taken place in other contexts about the need to prevent inappropriate third party access to confidential therapy notes. We will provide further updates in due course.

More generally, the controllers of a shared care record are required under the common law duty of confidentiality to communicate adequately to their local communities the existence and purposes of a shared care record, its impact on individuals and their right to object to some or all of their confidential patient information being included within that shared record.

Furthermore, the controllers of the shared care record must also ensure that they comply with UK General Data Protection Regulation requirements that data is processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, making reasonable efforts to ensure that individuals are informed about how their personal data is used.

In accordance with s251B of the Health and Social Care Act 2012, it is appropriate for clinicians to share information through a shared care record with other clinicians responsible for a patient’s care, unless that patient objects, or it is reasonable for them to believe that the patient would object. When it is necessary for direct care purposes, for example in an emergency situation, and those purposes are consistent with the reasonable expectations of the individual patient, health professionals will also rely on an assumption of consent to share essential information with other professionals responsible for the patient’s care.

However, as with all health records, there are strict rules and guidance in place to prevent unauthorised, inappropriate and unjustifiable access to confidential patient information by NHS employees, regardless of whether that information is held on a shared record, with staff who breach those rules facing suspension, dismissal and potential prosecution.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what plans they have, if any, to amend the Care Quality Commission's inspection framework or introduce legislative changes where appropriate, to ensure that cyber resilience is assessed as part of health and social care providers' responsibilities for safe care, operational continuity, governance and the protection of people's information.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) is a self-assessment toolkit that must be completed by health and social care providers to access National Health Service data. The DSPT’s requirements include a minimum data security training requirement for staff, organisational policies governing the use of personal devices, and the management of unsupported systems.

To support social care providers in strengthening their cyber security and resilience, the Department established the Better Security, Better Care (BSBC) programme in 2021. The programme provides guidance, training, and a dedicated helpline to help care providers complete the DSPT. The programme works with system partners, including the Care Quality Commission (CQC), to better ensure cyber security is prioritised across the adult social care sector. Alongside this support, care providers can also access the NHS Cyber Alerts service to receive up-to-date intelligence on potential cyber vulnerabilities, enabling them to take appropriate action.

Since the BSBC programme began in March 2021, the Department has invested £23 million in improving cyber resilience across the adult social care sector, with over 21,000 CQC registered care provider locations now completing the DSPT. Funding for the programme will continue until March 2029, supporting the adult social care sector to strengthen its cyber resilience as it progresses towards the Government’s ambition for a ‘fully digitised’ adult social care sector.

NHS England assures 23 digital social care record (DSCR) software solutions against core capabilities and a set of overarching standards. As part of this assurance, suppliers that deliver the assured DSCR solutions are required to meet several cyber security standards, including the DSPT, Cyber Essentials Plus, and ISO 27001. This gives social care providers greater confidence in the security of the digital solutions they use, supporting access to NHS services and enabling better care for people who draw on care and support. In addition to the work on cyber resilience delivery, the ambition for a ‘fully digitised’ sector also includes support to care providers to either migrate from existing legacy systems to assured DSCRs or to ensure that their legacy systems meet assurance requirements.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what recent steps she has taken to tackle online threats of (a) rape, (b) sexual abuse and (c) intimidation of women and girls through social media platforms.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
This Government recognises that technology can create new opportunities for perpetrators of VAWG, and we are committed to preventing and tackling abuse that occurs online.

In January 2024, the Online Safety Act introduced a threatening communications offence, which criminalised sending communications that threaten death, serious injury, and rape, where the sender intends for the recipient to fear that the threat will be carried out.

The Act requires also requires in-scope platforms, including social media platforms, to proactively tackle harmful and illegal content online. This includes proactively removing content that constitutes harassment, fear or provocation of violence, and sexual exploitation, all of which are priority offences.

The Home Office is investing in a pilot network of covert online officers to improve capabilities in identifying and targeting the most technologically sophisticated VAWG offenders. Insights gained from the pilot will be shared with Ofcom to help address the use of online platforms to cause harm.
writtenQuestions.heading: Gender Based Violence: Social Media

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what recent steps her Department has taken to tackle (a) online racial discrimination, (b) online religious discrimination and (c) other forms of online hate.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is determined to tackle all forms of hate crime, both online and offline. We have robust legislation in place to deal with threatening, abusive or harassing behaviour and the stirring up of racial and religious hatred. This includes communications offences under the Malicious Communications Act 1988 and Communications Act 2003, and the false and threatening communications offences in the Online Safety Act 2023.

Hate crime is also designated as a priority offence under the Online Safety Act 2023. Online services must take proactive steps to prevent their services being used to facilitate or commit such offences and have systems and processes in place to tackle illegal content.

The Government has increased funding to the police National Online Hate Crime Hub, providing £1.6 million per year to increase and improve the investigative capability of the police to tackle online hate. It also funds True Vision, which enables victims to report hate crime online.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what assessment he has made of the potential impact of Project Bromo, including the potential locating of Airbus’s Space Systems and Space Digital businesses as the UK component, on the level of UK jobs in the military satellite industry.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is assessing Project BROMO across relevant Departments, including its potential implications for the UK's space industrial base, national security, sovereign capabilities, critical skills, supply chains and employment.

The final structure and UK footprint of the proposed joint venture have not yet been determined, and it would therefore be premature to quantify its eventual impact on UK employment. writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what steps his Department is taking to support the development and implementation of the UK’s regulatory framework for digital assets.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government’s ambition is for the UK to become the global destination of choice for next-generation financial markets by 2030, while maintaining appropriate standards of consumer protection and market integrity.

As set out at Mansion House 2026, HM Treasury is supporting the development and implementation of the UK’s regulatory framework for digital assets through a comprehensive programme of work, working alongside the Bank of England, Financial Conduct Authority and industry. This work has three strategic pillars: cryptoassets and stablecoins, next-generation payments, and the digitalisation of wholesale financial markets.

On cryptoassets, we have established a comprehensive regulatory regime, including stablecoins, due to take effect from October 2027.

On Payments, the Financial Services and Markets Bill currently before Parliament seeks to give the Bank of England a secondary innovation objective in relation to its regulation of systemic payment systems and digital settlement asset service providers. This will support the Government's aim for the UK to remain at the forefront of innovation in payments and digital finance.

On wholesale markets, our focus is on moving from experimentation to wider adoption. The Digital Securities Sandbox (DSS) provides a modified regulatory environment in which firms can undertake live digital-asset activity. Seventeen firms have entered the Sandbox, with three firms authorised to conduct live activity and further authorisations expected. The Government has also tabled an amendment to the Financial Services and Markets Bill that would allow HM Treasury to update specified legislation to reflect technological change in financial market infrastructure and support the adoption and scaling of digital assets and tokenised markets.

We are also supporting the development of the wider market infrastructure needed for adoption, including working towards delivering the pilot of the Digital Gilt Instrument (DIGIT), which is set to take place by Q1 2027. The government appointed Christopher Woolard CBE as Wholesale Digital Markets Champion. His first report, published in July 2026 sets out priorities and recommendations for developing the UK’s tokenised wholesale markets which are now being taken forward.

writtenStatements.title: UK National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing
writtenStatements.text:
My right honourable friend the Economic Secretary to the Treasury (Lucy Rigby) has today made the following statement:

The proliferation of chemical, biological and nuclear weapons poses a serious and evolving threat to the United Kingdom's national security and to the wider international community. Proliferation financing (PF) remains central to the ability of hostile states and networks to procure materials, technology and expertise in support of illicit weapons programmes.

As a global financial centre and trading hub, the UK is exposed to indirect and inherent PF risks. This updated National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing (PF NRA), published on 23 November 2026, sets out the Government's assessment of those threats and vulnerabilities, building on the UK's first PF NRA published in 2021. The publication fulfils the requirement under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (the MLRs) to maintain an up-to-date assessment of UK proliferation financing risks.

Produced by HM Treasury, with contributions from across government, supervisors, law enforcement and academic experts, the assessment provides an updated and evidence-based overview of the proliferation financing risks facing the UK. It reflects significant developments since 2021, including the increasing sophistication of sanctions evasion and procurement networks, the growing use of cryptoassets and cyber-enabled activity, and enhancements to the UK's counter-proliferation financing framework.

The key findings of the PF NRA are:

  1. The UK’s financial sector remains at high risk from proliferators. The assessment concludes that the UK's proliferation financing risk remains largely indirect and inadvertent, principally arising from the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) and Iran-linked procurement and financing networks. The UK's position as a major international financial, trading and shipping centre means that legitimate financial and commercial activity may be exploited by proliferators seeking to generate revenue, procure goods and technology, or evade sanctions. The assessment finds that banking and payments, trade finance providers, insurers, legal and professional service providers, and virtual asset service providers remain particularly exposed to proliferation financing risks. It also highlights emerging threats, including the use of cryptoassets, cyber-enabled activity and DPRK-linked remote IT workers to generate revenue and evade sanctions.
  2. The DPRK and Iran remain the most significant proliferation financing actors at state level. Both continue to rely on procurement and financing networks to evade sanctions, generate revenue and acquire goods, technology and expertise in support of their weapons programmes.
  3. Despite these threats, the 2026 assessment finds that the UK has continued to strengthen its strategic, regulatory and operational capabilities to counter proliferation financing. This includes updating relevant sanctions regimes, introducing new export controls and corporate transparency measures, and requiring firms regulated under the MLRs to identify, assess and mitigate PF risk. Together, these measures enhance the UK’s ability to detect, prevent and disrupt proliferation financing activity, while supporting firms, as the first line of defence, to apply proportionate and risk-based controls.

The report is available at: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-risk-assessment-of-proliferation-financing-2026

This updated PF NRA demonstrates the UK's continued commitment to countering proliferation financing and protecting the integrity of the UK’s financial system. Since the publication of the first PF NRA in 2021, the UK has strengthened its counter-proliferation financing framework through enhancements to sanctions implementation and enforcement, export controls, corporate transparency and regulatory requirements on firms. The assessment supports the UK's wider national security objectives and reflects our continued leadership in international efforts to improve understanding of PF risks and strengthen implementation of Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards.
